Threat.value: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger
I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me
I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day

Memory.value: There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try
When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once
Fragments of the memory appear suddenly without warning and then disappear

Negative Appraisals.value: The people or institutions that should have protected me let me down

vignette:
Thanh, a fifty-year-old Vietnamese-American musician, spent most of his adult life performing in small jazz clubs across the city, his fingers finding comfort on the neck of his guitar. That comfort ended eighteen months ago when a woman who had attended three of his shows began waiting for him after every set, leaving notes on his car, and eventually following him home. The police called it nuisance behaviour and declined to file charges. The stalking escalated over six weeks until one night she broke into his apartment and stood in his bedroom doorway, whispering his name. Thanh froze. He could not move, could not speak, and afterwards could not remember how she left. That gap in his memory-the blank space between her shadow in the doorframe and the grey dawn light-has never returned. Fragments of that night still hit him without warning: the smell of her perfume, the weight of the silence, the way his throat locked shut. When these pieces arrive they are not memories; they are happening again, every sound and sensation exactly as real as the moment itself.

In the months that followed, Thanh came to see himself as fundamentally weak. He had not fought, had not even screamed. He told himself a real man would have done something. That judgment-that he was less than a man-kept dragging him back to the doorway, as if replaying the memory would somehow rewrite it, but each time it only played out the same frozen ending. This conviction that he was weak made the hole in his memory even more damning: every time the stalking scene surfaced without a clear ending, he interpreted the blankness as final proof that he had failed to protect himself. The numbness that settled over him felt like proof of this failure-he could not cry, could barely feel anger, only a deadened certainty that he was broken. At the same time, the institution he had trusted had let him down; the police had dismissed his fear, and that betrayal hardened into the belief that no one would help him, ever. Because he was weak, he reasoned, he could not protect himself, and because the system had failed, he was on his own. So he began to watch. Every stranger on the street became a potential threat. He studied their hands, their pace, the direction of their gaze. Yet the more hypervigilant he became, the more he read his own scanning as evidence that he was fundamentally incapable-a man so broken he had to treat every stranger as a threat, which only confirmed his certainty that he was irreparably weak. He avoided any neighbourhood he did not already know, refusing gigs in unfamiliar parts of town even though it cost him work. At night his vigilance sharpened-he slept with the lights on, checked the locks three times, and lay awake listening, the darkness itself feeling dangerous.

The watching and the avoiding were meant to keep him safe, but they also brought the memory closer. The more he scanned a crowd, the more likely a flash of long hair or a particular voice would trigger a sensory reliving, and then he would be back in that doorway, paralysed. Each reliving, in turn, confirmed his weakness: see, you still freeze, you still fail. And the numbness deepened, a kind of emotional desert where even the terror felt distant. Thanh had stopped playing music altogether. He cancelled his residency, stopped answering calls from bandmates, and spent most days on his sofa, windows shuttered against the afternoon light. His divorce-a decade old now-had left him isolated, but this was something worse: he had become a stranger to himself, a man who could not remember crucial parts of his own story and who could not trust the world enough to step outside.

What finally drove Thanh to request an appointment was a night last week when he tried to make himself go to a corner store two blocks from his apartment. He stood in his hallway for twenty minutes, heart hammering, convinced someone was watching from the end of the corridor. He could not move. The utter paralysis of that moment felt identical to the night of the stalking, and for the first time he understood that his life had shrunk to a single room. He is terrified that this will never change-that the weakness is permanent, that the memory will keep flooding back, and that the institution that failed him once will fail him again. But beneath the numbness, something else is stirring: a fragile hope that someone might finally hear what happened and not turn away.
